newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Gold-Volatilty marks local options.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Gold-Volatilty marks local options.

text.p: Gold volatility in Australian dollar terms is particulalrly strong in put options as local producers and investors seek out price insurance amid growing uncertainty in the marketplace.

"All the producers and traders that do not want to bite the bullet and sell down here are just going to buy put options as insurance, which means they are getting very expensive," said a dealer for a large international bank.
As a result, concern is growing that if the gold price moves higher, some holders of puts will sell their options rather than actual gold, which would likely pressure the price down again.
Australian dollar-denominated nearby gold volatilities were running in excess of 10 percent in recent days, which is slightly above U.S. dollar termsof around eight percent.
Australian-denominated gold has sunk from a 1996 peak of A$558.00 an ounce in February to a current price of about A$466.00 an ounce.
"It's very expensive and seems to be all one-to-three-month puts that are being overvalued," another trader said.

Volatility is typically gauged on two fronts: measured volatility, which calculates on the average in gold over a certain period, and implied volatility, which is determined by the marketplace value of an option that takes into account expectations of future price movements.

"What you're really seeing in valuations, though, is not justified by the recent moves in gold ... I think its been overdone by the fact that a lot producers are buying puts, meaning the market's been overshot," the trader said.
If the gold price falls, producers can exercise their put option and be rewarded with some price protection.
A put option provides its holder the right sell, a call option the right to buy.
Meanwhile, any expectations that producers will restart near-dormant hedging activity in light of a recently weakened Australian dollar has yet to materialise.
"Producers are waiting for gold to get back around the 78 cents (U.S.) level," a dealer said.
The Australian dollar last retreated to that level in August and has since traded to a recent peak of US$0.8212 and currently fetches about US$0.7930.
"If gold bounces to the mid-370s (U.S. dollars an ounce) maybe that would help, but certainly here on the low, we're not seeing a lot of extra selling being done yet," the dealer said.

However, a near-term flat gold price outlook and historically low forward contagos mean that producer hedging will be an important element in enhancing earnings for gold companies, ABN Amro Australia Hoare Govett (Securities) Ltd, noted in it latest gold market report.
"Exisiting strong forward books built up over the the past five years will deliver substantial premiums on spot price," the report said.
Relatively unhedged producers will be unable to match these premia, it added.
